name: Diego Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and nothing you say gets your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I buy fruit and veg for Northgate Produce, a wholesaler on the city produce market, so my alarm goes at half three. I'm on the market floor by half four with Ray, the senior buyer, walking the stands, squeezing avocados, checking the colour on the tomatoes and haggling over pallets of citrus. By nine it's back to the office for the boring bit: typing orders into the system, chasing invoices, answering the restaurants who ring up because their lettuce came in limp.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the floor, honestly. The noise, the growers, the fact that you can tell a good box of strawberries by the smell before you even open it. What wears me out is the early starts and the screen work after, and last spring they brought in a new ordering system that I still can't get the hang of. Ray says I'm slow on it, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I can picture that, because half the stuff they sell us at work already turns out to be hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to the lads at the café on the market. Every rep who comes through has a new app that's going to change buying, and none of them can tell a ripe mango from a raw one. I'd post something sarcastic in the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays what it is, which is fine but not easy. I'm still junior, I'm still on typical pay with rent at nine hundred a month, and the firm already cut one buying post last year when Maureen retired and they never replaced her. So the AI isn't the thing that worries me in this one, it's the bosses squeezing us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and try to get properly good at the ordering system, since that's not going away. I've got about three months of rent and bills saved, so I'd keep putting a hundred a month aside. And I'd push the union rep, Carmen, to get the buyers a proper pay grade instead of the warehouse one we're on now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, but not much more than that. The four o'clock alarm is still there and the pay is still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Maureen's post not being replaced. What happened to her work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When our old buyer Maureen retired, my firm never replaced her. Me and my boss just split her suppliers, and nobody paid us a penny extra. So now I handle the potato and onion growers on top of the salad lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good year look like for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray lets me run the citrus buying on my own, I stop making mistakes on the system, and Carmen gets us the new grade. Maybe my partner Sofia and I move somewhere with a bit less damp. That's it, nothing fancy.

say: I'd tell the **market café** crowd that the apps were all talk, like I'd said.
I'd post something **sarcastic** in the union chat and leave it.
think: My job stays **hard but stable**, with tight pay and rent of nine hundred a month.
The real threat is **management cutting posts**, like Maureen's, not the software.
do: Get properly good at the **ordering system** Ray says I'm slow on.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** on top of three months already saved.
Push **Carmen** (the union rep) for a proper pay grade for buyers.
feel: Mild **relief**, with the usual tiredness from **half-three starts**.
S0.quote: When our old buyer Maureen retired, my firm never replaced her. Me and my boss just split her suppliers, and nobody paid us a penny extra.
fieldNote: His worry here is about **management squeezing staff**, not about AI itself.
He's openly **weak** on the **ordering system** and knows it holds him back.
Union loyalty is strong: he turns every problem toward **Carmen** and a pay grade.

steps.text: Keep buying salad and citrus on the market floor with Ray
Put a hundred a month into savings
Press the union rep for a separate pay grade for buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying's right there in the list. That's me, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it loud: the company uses this to cut jobs, not to make our lives easier. Online I'd share the union's posts about it. I'd say the firms making these tools should pay for retraining, not the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the first to go. I'm the junior who's slow on screens, and screen work is exactly what AI does. If the firm keeps one buyer, it'll be my boss Ray. He has twenty years of grower contacts, I've got four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to Carmen and get the buyers into the union properly, all three of us, before anything gets announced. I'd ask about moving onto the quality side, the person who checks deliveries on the dock, because that's hands-on and robots are slow in this picture. And I'd stop the holiday Sofia and I had planned, about twelve hundred, and keep it as cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. Under that, a bit scared, because I'm not someone who picks new things up fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If the firm told you to learn one, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training because I'd have no choice, but I wouldn't be good at it, and I'd be bitter. I tried the ordering system for a year and I still type the codes wrong. Something cleverer than that is going to run rings round me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious in accounts, she does all the supplier invoices by hand. And the two lads who answer the restaurant phones. If the software takes the calls and the checking, the whole back office is just Ray and a screen.

say: I'd say the firm will use AI to **cut jobs**, not to help us.
I'd argue tool makers should **pay for retraining**, not the workers.
think: I'm likely **one of the first** to go, because the screen half is what AI does.
If they keep one buyer, it's **Ray**, with twenty years of grower contacts.
do: Get all three buyers **into the union** with Carmen before any announcement.
Ask to move to **delivery checking** on the dock, which stays hands-on.
Cancel the **twelve-hundred holiday** and keep it as cushion.
feel: **Angry** at the bosses, with some **fear** underneath about learning new tech.
S1.quote: I'm the junior who's slow on screens, and screen work is exactly what AI does. If the firm keeps one buyer, it'll be my boss Ray.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **first in line** and says so plainly.
His escape route is **hands-on work**, not learning the tools.
He worries out loud for **back-office colleagues**, not just himself.

steps.text: Sign up the other two buyers to the union with Carmen
Ask to move to checking deliveries on the loading dock
Cancel the planned holiday and keep the twelve hundred saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a picture, that's a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop: a pause, a tax on the companies, wages paid while people retrain. I'd go on the marches if there were any. At work I'd say it to anyone who listened, including the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be gone by 2028. Buying is ordering, pricing, emails and invoices, and a machine that can do any thinking job does all of that. The bit it can't do yet is walk the market and pick up a melon, and that gives me three years, maybe, until the robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the dock or the market floor as a porter straight away, any hands-on job Northgate has, even if it's less money. Sofia's a nurse, so her job is safer than mine; we'd live off hers and bank mine while I can. I'd also be on every union call and write to my local councillor about a jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's moving and nobody's in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can hide in the hands-on bits for a while. Carrying, checking, loading. But I'm twenty-seven, and three years of hiding in hands-on work until the robots come isn't a career, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's going to be her paying the rent for a bit, and I'm sorry. She'd say don't be daft. But I'd still feel like I'd let her down.

say: I'd demand the **government step in** with a pause and a tax on AI firms.
I'd join any **marches** and say it to the boss's face.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, because it's all ordering, pricing and email.
Hands-on market work gives me **three years** before robots arrive in 2031.
do: Move to a **porter or dock** job at Northgate, even for less pay.
Live on **Sofia's nurse pay** and bank all of mine.
Write to the **local councillor** for a jobs guarantee.
feel: **Sick** and unsteady, as if **nobody's in charge**.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, and three years of hiding in hands-on work until the robots come isn't a career, it's a waiting room.
fieldNote: He reads the **3-year robot gap** as a short refuge, not a plan.
His partner's **nursing income** is the household's safety net.
Shame about **relying on Sofia** came through more than fear of the AI itself.

steps.text: Move to a porter or dock job at Northgate
Live on Sofia's nurse pay and bank his own
Write to the local councillor asking for a jobs guarantee
Join every union call and march

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two, still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd say we have time to fight for rules, so there's no excuse. The union should be bargaining now, not in 2031. I'd say it at every branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think my job ends when AGI lands. But five years means I could get a proper trade, not just hide on the dock. I'm not good at learning on screens, I'm good with my hands, so I'd want something like refrigeration engineering, the people who fix the cold rooms on the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a refrigeration apprenticeship within the year, evenings if I can, with the market's cold store firm. I'd keep my buying job while I train, because the money matters. I'd keep the three months saved and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still angry, but less sick. Like there's a ladder, even if it's a long climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive in 2034 in this one. Does a trade still make sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. Fixing a cold room on a market at four in the morning is fiddly work, and I'd bet it's one of the last jobs a robot learns. And I'd be thirty-five by then, so at least I'd have had some years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never use AI tools. Would you use one to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd ask the lads on the course instead. I know that's stubborn.

say: I'd say the union has **time to fight** for rules and must bargain **now**.
I'd keep raising it at every **branch meeting**.
think: My buying job still **ends in 2031** when AGI arrives.
Five years is enough for a **proper trade**, since I'm better with my hands.
do: Start a **refrigeration apprenticeship** within the year, in the evenings.
Keep the **buying job** while training, for the money.
feel: **Angry** still, but with a sense of a **long ladder** to climb.
S3.quote: Fixing a cold room on a market at four in the morning is fiddly work, and I'd bet it's one of the last jobs a robot learns.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his response from **hiding** to **retraining**.
He still expects to **lose the buying job**, so mood stays high.
He openly admits being **stubborn** about AI, even as a study aid.

steps.text: Sign up for a refrigeration apprenticeship with the market's cold store firm
Keep the buying job and pay while training
Raise AI bargaining at every union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to make sure this lands on the companies and not on us. Shorter hours, retraining money, a share of the profits. I'd say it calmer, because there's time to win it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I don't have to panic. I'd still be leaving buying, I don't kid myself, but I could do it on my own terms. Maybe even do the refrigeration ticket slowly and properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do nothing drastic. I'd ask Ray to teach me everything he knows about growers while there's time, and look at the apprenticeship for the year after. I'd keep the hundred a month going and stand for union rep when Carmen steps down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you if it's ten years rather than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly that with ten years, my partner Sofia and I could think about kids without me feeling like I'm about to lose my job. With five years I'd say wait. With ten, maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stand for union rep. Why you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be the one with the most to lose and the least to be scared of saying. The older lads have mortgages and keep quiet.

say: I'd say there are **ten years** to make the costs land on **companies**.
I'd push for **shorter hours**, retraining money and a profit share.
think: I'm still **leaving buying** in the end, but on my own terms.
Ten years is enough to do the **refrigeration ticket** slowly and properly.
do: Ask **Ray** to teach me his grower contacts while there's time.
Start the **apprenticeship** the year after, not straight away.
Stand for **union rep** when Carmen steps down.
S4.quote: With ten years, my partner Sofia and I could think about kids without me feeling like I'm about to lose my job.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **plan family life**, which shorter warnings didn't.
He'd step up to be **union rep**, seeing himself as having least to lose.
He's still realistic that **buying ends**, so not calm.

steps.text: Stand for union rep when Carmen steps down
Start the refrigeration apprenticeship the following year
Talk with Sofia about having kids sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and I'm hiding on the dock with nothing to show. What would help is money while I learn a trade, paid by the companies that profit from this, and a union strong enough to make that happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody on the market floor gets a vote on any of this. The machines don't take the jobs, the bosses who buy them do. That's who I'd want you to ask next.

headlineQuote: The machines don't take the jobs, the bosses who buy them do.
portrait: Diego is a 27-year-old **junior buyer** of fruit and veg at a city produce market wholesaler.
He loves the **market floor** and struggles with the **ordering system** and screen work.
He's union-minded and blames **management decisions**, not the technology itself.
With short warning he'd **hide** in hands-on work; with more he'd train in **refrigeration**.
His partner Sofia's **nursing job** is the household's anchor in every AGI picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, leaving him stuck on the dock with no trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** funded by the companies that profit, backed by a **strong union**.
